title: Not the spirit of the Stoics
source_text: Ὡς μὴ νοήσας δὴ τὰ περὶ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ Κέλσος („ψυχικὸς γὰρ ἄνθρωπος οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ θεοῦ· μωρία γὰρ αὐτῷ ἐστι, καὶ οὐ δύναται γνῶναι, ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται“) ἑαυτῷ συνάπτει, οἰόμενος ἡμᾶς λέγοντας „πνεῦμα“ εἶναι τὸν θεὸν μηδὲν ἐν τούτῳ διαφέρειν τῶν παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι Στωϊκῶν, φασκόντων ὅτι ὁ θεὸς πνεῦμά ἐστι διὰ πάντων διεληλυθὸς καὶ πάντ᾿ ἐν ἑαυτῷ περιέχον. διήκει μὲν γὰρ ἡ ἐπισκοπὴ καὶ ἡ πρόνοια τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ πάντων ἀλλ᾿ οὐχ ὡς τὸ τῶν Στωϊκῶν πνεῦμα· καὶ πάντα μὲν περιέχει τὰ προνοούμενα ἡ πρόνοια καὶ περιείληφεν αὐτὰ, οὐχ ὡς σῶμα δὲ περιέχον περιέχει, ὅτε καὶ σῶμά ἐστι τὸ περιεχόμενον, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς δύναμις θεία καὶ περιειληφυῖα τὰ περιεχόμενα. κατὰ μὲν οὖν τοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς, σωματικὰς λέγοντας εἶναι τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πάντα φθείροντας κινδυνεύοντας δὲ καὶ αὐτὸν φθεῖραι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν, εἰ μὴ πάνυ ἀπεμφαῖνον τοῦτ᾿ αὐτοῖς ἐδόκει τυγχάνειν, καὶ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ ὁ μέχρι ἀνθρώπων καὶ τῶν ἐλαχίστων καταβαίνων οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ πνεῦμα σωματικόν· κατὰ δὲ ἡμᾶς καὶ τὴν λογικὴν ψυχὴν πειρωμένους ἀποδεικνύναι κρείττονα πάσης σωματικῆς φύσεως καὶ οὐσίαν ἀόρατον καὶ ἀσώματον οὐκ ἂν σῶμα εἴη ὁ θεὸς λόγος, δι᾿ οὗ τὰ πάντ᾿ ἐγένετο, ὁ φθάνων, ἵνα πάντα διὰ λόγου γίνηται, οὐχ ἕως ἀνθρώπων μόνων ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν ἐλαχίστων εἶναι νομιζομένων καὶ ὑπὸ φύσεως διοικουμένων. πάντα μὲν οὖν οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς ἐκπυρούτωσαν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀσώματον οὐσίαν οὐκ ἴσμεν ἐκπυρουμένην οὐδ᾿ εἰς πῦρ ἀναλυομένην τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν ἢ τὴν ἀγγέλων ἢ θρόνων ἢ κυριοτήτων ἢ ἀρχῶν ἢ ἐξουσιῶν ὑπόστασιν.
pass_a_gloss: As not having understood (νοέω) indeed the things about the Spirit of God, Celsus ('for the natural/soulish (ψυχικός) man does not receive (δέχομαι) the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness (μωρία) to him, and he cannot know, because it is spiritually (πνευματικῶς) discerned (ἀνακρίνω)') joins on (συνάπτω) for himself, thinking that we, saying God is 'spirit', in this differ (διαφέρω) in nothing from the Stoics among the Greeks, asserting (φάσκω) that God is spirit having passed through (διέρχομαι) all things and containing (περιέχω) all things in itself. For the oversight (ἐπισκοπή) and providence (πρόνοια) of God does pervade (διήκω) through all things, but not as the spirit of the Stoics; and providence contains all the things provided for (προνοέω) and has embraced (περιλαμβάνω) them, not as a containing body contains, when also the contained is a body, but as divine power (δύναμις θεία) and having embraced the contained. According, then, to those from the Stoa (Στοά), saying the first principles (ἀρχαί) are bodily (σωματικός) and on this account making all things perishable (φθείρω) and risking (κινδυνεύω) to make perishable even the God over all himself, if this did not seem to them altogether incongruous (ἀπεμφαίνω), even the Word of God coming down (καταβαίνω) as far as men and the least things (ἐλάχιστα) is nothing other than bodily spirit; but according to us, trying (πειράω) to demonstrate (ἀποδείκνυμι) even the rational soul (λογικὴ ψυχή) superior (κρείττων) to all bodily nature and an invisible (ἀόρατος) and incorporeal (ἀσώματος) substance (οὐσία), God the Word would not be body, through whom all things came to be, he who reaches (φθάνω), so that all things come to be through the Word, not to men only but also to the things thought (νομίζω) to be least and administered (διοικέω) by nature (φύσις). Let those from the Stoa then consume all things in conflagration (ἐκπυρόω); but we know (οἶδα) no incorporeal substance being burned up, nor dissolved (ἀναλύω) into fire the soul of man or the subsistence (ὑπόστασις) of angels or thrones (θρόνοι) or dominions (κυριότητες) or principalities (ἀρχαί) or powers (ἐξουσίαι).
pass_b_english: Since, then, Celsus did not understand the things of the Spirit of God (“for the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot know them, because they are spiritually discerned,” 1 Corinthians 2:14), he draws an inference of his own, thinking that when we say God is “spirit,” we differ in nothing on this point from the Stoics among the Greeks, who claim that God is a spirit that has passed through all things and holds all things within itself.

Now the oversight and providence of God do pass through all things, but not in the way the spirit of the Stoics does. And providence does hold within it all the things it provides for, and embraces them; but it does not hold them as a body holds, when what is held is also a body, but as a divine power that has embraced what it holds.

According to the men of the Stoa, who say that the first principles are bodily, and for this reason make all things perishable, and who come close to making perishable even the God who is over all, had this not seemed to them utterly absurd, even the Word of God, who comes down as far as men and the very least things, is nothing other than a bodily spirit. But according to us, who try to prove that even the rational soul is higher than every bodily nature, and is an invisible and incorporeal substance, God the Word, through whom all things came to be (John 1:3), would not be a body. He reaches not only as far as men but also to the things thought to be the least and governed by nature, so that all things may come to be through the Word.

Let the men of the Stoa, then, burn up all things in their world-conflagration; but we know of no incorporeal substance that is burned up, nor do we know that the soul of man, or the being of angels or thrones or dominions or principalities or powers (Colossians 1:16), is dissolved into fire.

choices.choice: 1 Corinthians 2:14 is quoted in a parenthesis in the Greek; the parenthesis is kept. ψυχικός rendered ‘natural’ (the man who lives by soul alone). The Stoic formula ‘a spirit that has passed through all things and holds all things within itself’ is reported indirectly and may echo Celsus’s words, but the Greek does not mark it as a quotation, so it is not in quotation marks. ἑαυτῷ συνάπτει rendered ‘he draws an inference of his own’ (he joins on a conclusion of his own making). κινδυνεύοντας ... φθεῖραι: the Stoics ‘come close to’ making God perishable. ὁ φθάνων clause reordered into natural English: ‘He reaches ... so that all things may come to be through the Word’. ἐκπυρούτωσαν rendered ‘burn up all things in their world-conflagration’ (the Stoic ekpyrosis); ἐκπυρουμένην ‘burned up’, keeping the same verb. ‘Being’ renders ὑπόστασις. Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers in the order of Colossians 1:16. ‘Through whom all things came to be’ is John 1:3 (πάντα δι᾿ αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο).
'he goes on, on his own account' to 'he draws an inference of his own' (ἑαυτῷ συνάπτει; awkward 'on, on')

'He reaches, so that all things may come to be through the Word, not only as far as men' reordered to 'He reaches not only as far as men but also to ..., so that all things may come to be through the Word' (stiff Greek order)
'give everything over to the great burning' to 'burn up all things in their world-conflagration' ('great' was added; ἐκπυρόω kept as one verb)
'consumed by fire' to 'burned up' (ἐκπυρουμένην, same verb as the Stoic conflagration)
